segments.text: In 1902, the city of Hanoi had a serious problem on its hands. Swarms of rats had completely
infested their brand new sewer system, creating a massive public health crisis. To fix it,
the authorities devised what looked like a perfectly logical plan. They offered citizens
a cash bounty for every severed rat tail they turned in. The underlying assumption
was completely straightforward. One tail equals one dead rat. The tail was undeniable physical
proof of the deed. And at first, the program worked exactly as intended. Thousands of tails
poured in, and the government happily paid out the bounties. Then, people across the city started
reporting a very strange sight. Healthy rats roaming the streets, going about their business,
entirely missing their tails. The rat hunters had figured out a better way to play the game.
Instead of killing their catch, they trapped the rats, clipped their tails for the cash,
and tossed them right back into the sewers to breed. The economic logic was flawless. A dead
rat pays out exactly once. A living rat, having babies, is a permanent income stream. Some highly
entrepreneurial citizens took this logic to its absolute limit, setting up dedicated rat farms to
ensure they would never run out of inventory. By the time the government realized what was
happening and canceled the program, they were left holding a mountain of severed tails,
and Hanoi had a larger rat population than when the bounties started. Put a simple,
highly logical plan into a world full of humans reacting to incentives, and you will almost
certainly turn the intended solution into an entirely new set of problems. This pattern
of human behavior warping perfectly good plans didn't stop in 1902. If we look at modern
history, we see a massive gap between what creators expected to happen and how things
actually played out. This infographic highlights four specific examples of that gap, tracking
exactly how initial plans mutated. Take early SMS messaging. It was originally built with a very
limited scope, so mobile networks could send short, one-way alerts down to their subscribers.
But young people quickly co-opted the feature, turning texting into a two-way conversation and
the primary way we stay in touch every day. Or look at GPS. It was designed strictly as a
military tool to help armed forces pinpoint locations and navigate the globe. Today, it
facilitates civilian ride-sharing and food deliveries. Even more critically, the precise
timing mechanisms inside GPS satellites are now required to keep our global phone networks,
banks, and power grids operational. When it comes to technology, the engineers might write the code,
but the end users ultimately decide how the tool gets used in the real world. The same
rule applies to biology. Australia imported non-native cane toads with a highly specific job. Eat the
beetles that were destroying their valuable sugar cane crops. The toads barely ate the
targeted pests. Instead, they poisoned native wildlife and spread uncontrollably across the
entire continent. It happens with massive infrastructure too. The city of Houston spent
$2.8 billion to widen the Katy Freeway, fully expecting all that new concrete to ease traffic
congestion. The data shows the exact opposite happened. Between 2011 and 2014, rush hour trips
actually grew 30 to 55 percent longer because the newly created road space simply encouraged more
people to drive. Whether we are tweaking an ecosystem or pouring billions of dollars into
asphalt, complex systems consistently react to our interventions in ways that defeat the
original plan. Which brings us to the current development of artificial intelligence. We have
an unbroken historical record of actual outcomes deviating wildly from initial expectations.
Because of that, projecting the long-term future based purely on today's blueprints is largely
useless. Because of that dynamic, the highly confident predictions we are currently hearing
from both AI optimists and AI warriors are probably wrong. Nobody can accurately map
exactly where this technology will land, and its final impact on society will look vastly different
from what the public expects today. The single most consequential thing AI does in your lifetime,
whether positive or negative, is likely an application that no one in any lab,
university course, or tech company has even thought of yet. That inherent uncertainty isn't
a reason to panic. It is the primary reason we have to remain highly attentive to how the
technology is actually being used. As the banner in this image shows, some of the biggest historical
shifts are always the ones that defied prediction. Navigating a completely unknowable future
requires attention. And that is the best reason to stay curious.
